effect_mechanism: In low- and lower-middle-income settings the pooled per-hectare costs are up-front establishment and treatment costs. An independent evaluation of two World Bank-supported India watershed projects reports treatment unit costs of US$261 per hectare in the Integrated Watershed Development Project and US$217/ha in the Karnataka project [ev_project_cost_iegind11_10, ev_project_cost_iegind11_11]. A Yemen completion report gives average investment costs for spate systems of USD 800- 1200/ha, of which the farmer's 15-20% share comes to US$ 150-200/ha [ev_project_cost_yem12_8]. Two WOCAT technology sheets add compiler-reported establishment costs: 2000.00 USD per hectare for orchard terraces in Uzbekistan, a total spread over 1.6 ha [ev_project_cost_wocat_7553_2025_establishment], and 147.30 USD per hectare for gabion and rock check-dam gully control in Somalia, a total spread over 160 ha [ev_project_cost_wocat_7778_2026_establishment].
conditionality: The figures measure different things: watershed treatment cost per hectare treated in India, spate-system investment in Yemen, and WOCAT compilers' own cost tables converted with each sheet's exchange rate, which are not market prices; none is a cost per hectare of degraded land restored, and no price-year adjustment is made across them. The India evaluator calls the US$261 per hectare cost high by Indian standards, and the US$217/ha cost below the central government norm [ev_project_cost_iegind11_10, ev_project_cost_iegind11_11]; the Yemen report calls the farmer contribution comparatively high [ev_project_cost_yem12_8]. The Somali figure spreads a whole gully-control package over the treated area, which keeps it low per hectare, while the Uzbek terrace figure is a small orchard plot, so the spread from 147.30 to 2000.00 USD per hectare reflects practice and denominator as much as cost. All four countries are in the low- or lower-middle-income target band.

effect_mechanism: Pooled units describe how siting and implementer affect what structures cost: in Karnataka, land-resource-inventory planning avoided unnecessary structures and lowered the construction cost of soil and water conservation works per hectare versus a conventional programme; in Ghana, the share of small dams rehabilitated below given per-irrigated-hectare cost thresholds differed between government and donor/NGO implementers. Field trials add on-farm savings: no-till with a residue mulch reduced total variable costs by 5% against conventional tillage in a Zimbabwe trial, and mulching reduced weed density and labour costs for weeding in an Ethiopian trial [ev_project_cost_mash25h1_5, ev_project_cost_sime15h2_1].
conditionality: Both are from lower-middle-income countries but measure different things: the India figure is an absolute construction cost per hectare from a lender completion report (the saving is relative to another SWC programme, not to no intervention), and the Ghana figure is a distribution of dam rehabilitation costs by implementer, not a cost reduction. What separates the sides: the reductions are each a comparison with an alternative on the same land (the Karnataka planning against a conventional programme, the trial plots against conventional tillage or no mulch), while the Ghana unit sits on the other side only as a spread of rehabilitation costs between implementers, with no comparison against doing otherwise. The Zimbabwe saving is for mulch bundled with no-till, and the Ethiopian saving is a weeding-labour statement without a figure [ev_project_cost_mash25h1_5, ev_project_cost_sime15h2_1].

justification.statement: water_harvesting_conservation cost_reduction: CONFLICTING EVIDENCE — material weight on both the benefit and the harm side, so no direction is stated. This is not a null finding: studies found real effects, in opposite directions, and the agreement note lists both sides. Read the conditionality for what separates them (transfer: in_context).

Field trials add on-farm savings: no-till with a residue mulch reduced total variable costs by 5% against conventional tillage in a Zimbabwe trial, and mulching reduced weed density and labour costs for weeding in an Ethiopian trial [ev_project_cost_mash25h1_5, ev_project_cost_sime15h2_1].
justification.conditionality: Both are from lower-middle-income countries but measure different things: the India figure is an absolute construction cost per hectare from a lender completion report (the saving is relative to another SWC programme, not to no intervention), and the Ghana figure is a distribution of dam rehabilitation costs by implementer, not a cost reduction. What separates the sides: the reductions are each a comparison with an alternative on the same land (the Karnataka planning against a conventional programme, the trial plots against conventional tillage or no mulch), while the Ghana unit sits on the other side only as a spread of rehabilitation costs between implementers, with no comparison against doing otherwise. The Zimbabwe saving is for mulch bundled with no-till, and the Ethiopian saving is a weeding-labour statement without a figure [ev_project_cost_mash25h1_5, ev_project_cost_sime15h2_1].
